justice: Both sides of the street provide pedestrian space: a wide, paved sidewalk on the right and a narrower walking edge on the left, indicating relatively equitable allocation beyond vehicle lanes.
Street furniture exists for public use (bench seating on the right), supporting fair access to resting space for different users rather than private-only amenities.

Accessibility appears mixed: the right-side sidewalk looks continuous and step-free along the block, but no clear curb ramps or tactile paving are visible at crossing points in this view, limiting full barrier-free accessibility for all users.
safety: No protected bike lane or physical cycling separation is visible; cyclists likely share the motor lane, increasing conflict risk with vehicles and delivery tricycles/scooters seen ahead.
Pedestrian walking space on the right is partially encroached by parked scooters/bikes near the storefronts, creating obstacles that can force pedestrians closer to the curb edge.

Marked vehicle direction arrows and relatively low apparent traffic volume improve predictability, but the long, straight roadway can still encourage higher speeds without visible traffic-calming elements (e.g., raised crossings, chicanes).
livability: Active ground-floor frontage on the right (commercial building with frequent entrances) supports everyday services and street vitality.
Public seating (bench and small stools/tables near the shopfront) enables lingering and social interaction, improving street life.
Presence of pedestrians along both sides and clustered activity near storefronts suggests the street supports daily walking and local commerce.
sustainability: Street trees and planted areas (tree pits/planters along the right and greenery in the median/edge planting on the left) add urban green infrastructure benefits.
High levels of scooter/bicycle presence near the right-hand shops suggest some reliance on lower-carbon micromobility for access.
However, the streetscape still prioritizes paved surfaces and motor roadway; no visible transit stop facilities or dedicated cycling infrastructure reduces the modal shift potential.
aesthetics: The right-side architecture has a coherent, modern streetscape with consistent facade lines and large windows, creating visual order.
Greenery (street trees and planters) softens the street edge and adds color/texture, improving perceived quality.
Overall cleanliness and organized street lighting poles contribute to a tidy, legible streetscape, though scattered parked scooters can add visual clutter.
comfort: Thermal comfort is moderate: some tree canopy exists but is limited, and much of the sidewalk appears exposed to direct sun in this image.
Physical comfort is supported by smooth, wide paving on the right and the presence of a bench, but comfort is reduced where scooters/bikes occupy pedestrian space near storefronts.

Psychological comfort is helped by active frontage and multiple pedestrians (natural surveillance), but mixed micromobility and vehicle movement in the same corridor can create stress for cautious users.
walkability: The right sidewalk is wide and continuous, supporting two-way pedestrian flow and passing/lingering near shops.
Street lighting poles and clear curb definition improve edge legibility for pedestrians, aiding navigation.
Walkability is weakened by sidewalk encroachment from parked scooters/bikes and by limited visible safe crossing infrastructure within the frame (no marked crosswalk nearby).
bikeability: No dedicated or protected bike lane markings are visible; cyclists appear to ride in the general traffic lane, lowering perceived safety and comfort.
Potential door/merging conflicts exist near the right curb where many scooters/bikes are parked and where pedestrians are active at storefront edges.
Lack of visible bike-specific signals, intersection treatments, or clearly designated bicycle parking reduces cycling convenience and network clarity.
